title: Lab 01 — Two-Subnet Office LAN
subtitle: Junior network engineer portfolio · Cisco Packet Tracer
summary: A small office with Sales and Ops on two /26 subnets, joined by a single 2911 router. Built in Packet Tracer with IOS CLI, a security baseline, verification, and four break/fix scenarios.
imageAlt: Cisco Packet Tracer logical topology: R1 (2911) connects SW1 (Sales) and SW2 (Ops), each with two PCs.

blocks.text: A small office has two departments, Sales and Ops. Each department needs its own subnet so traffic and broadcasts stay separated. A single router connects the two subnets so the departments can still talk to each other.

items: Devices: Cisco 2911 (R1), two 2960-24TT switches (SW1, SW2), four PCs
Cabling: copper straight-through (unlike devices: PC to switch, switch to router)
No static or dynamic routing — R1 is directly connected to both subnets

blocks.text: Requirement: two equal subnets with at least 60 usable hosts each. 2^6 = 64 addresses (62 usable) → 6 host bits → /26. Mask 255.255.255.192; block size 64. Spare .128/26 and .192/26 are left unused for growth.

rows: show ip int brief on R1
Two C and two L routes
Replies (first run may drop 1–2 packets while ARP resolves)

blocks.text:
192.168.10.0/24 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 2 masks
C    192.168.10.0/26 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L    192.168.10.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C    192.168.10.64/26 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L    192.168.10.65/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1

rows: Ping timed out. R1 routes the request over, but PC-B2 cannot reply to another subnet without a gateway. Same-subnet pings still work.
Destination host unreachable. R1 loses its connected route to 10.64/26; show ip int brief shows administratively down. Fix: no shutdown.
Wrong mask on PC-A2 (/24 instead of /26)
With /24, PC-A2 thinks .74 is local and ARPs on LAN-A instead of using the gateway. Restore 255.255.255.192.
Unlike devices use straight-through. Packet Tracer may still bring Gi links up (Auto-MDIX); the exam still tests the cable rule.

items: Console, VTY, and enable passwords are separate — VTY needs its own password.
A switch needs a default gateway only for remote management; its ports forward on MAC address (Layer 2). The mgmt SVI exists so you can reach the switch itself.
If Sales grows to 100 hosts it needs /25 (.0–.127), which overlaps Ops' .64/26 — Ops would move to .128/26.
Router ports are off by default; no shutdown brings them up. Amber switch links are Spanning Tree settling — wait for green.

blocks.text: Open lab01.pkt in Cisco Packet Tracer to walk the same topology. Full IOS configs and the lab guide live in the GitHub repo — lab passwords are for this lab only, never production.

imageCaption: Packet Tracer Logical workspace: Sales (SW1) and Ops (SW2) meet at R1.

title: Lab 02 — Centralized DHCP with Relay Agents
subtitle: Junior network engineer portfolio · Cisco Packet Tracer
status: Part 1 of 2 · static routing + DHCP relay (Miami lease test in progress)
summary: Three sites joined by /30 point-to-point links. Miami and New York have no local DHCP server: each city router relays DHCP requests across the WAN to a server in the data center. Covers DORA, giaddr, scopes, static routing, and a real troubleshooting log.
imageAlt: Cisco Packet Tracer logical workspace: Router-MIA, Router-NY, and Router-DC joined by /30 links; SW-DC connects DHCP-MIA and DHCP-NY; each city has a switch and three PCs.
imageCaption: Packet Tracer logical workspace. Router-DC (ISR4331) links to Router-MIA and Router-NY over RN2 and RN3; RN1 joins the two branches. DHCP-MIA and DHCP-NY sit behind SW-DC.

blocks.text: A company has a data center (DC) and two branch cities, Miami and New York. Each branch LAN needs its addresses assigned automatically, but the DHCP servers live in the data center so administration stays in one place.

items: Three Cisco routers: Router-DC, Router-MIA, and Router-NY, joined in a triangle by /30 links.
Two DHCP servers on the DC LAN: 192.168.50.10 serves Miami and 192.168.50.20 serves New York.
Each branch router acts as a DHCP relay agent for its LAN.
Routing is static in this part. Dynamic routing is Part 2.

blocks.text: Why a relay is needed: a PC with no address sends a DHCP Discover as a broadcast. Routers do not forward broadcasts, so the request would die at the branch router. The relay agent (ip helper-address) catches it and forwards it as a unicast to the server.
A /30 has four addresses and two usable, which is exactly what a point-to-point router link needs. A /26 gives each city 62 usable hosts and splits 192.168.0.0/24 into clean 64-address blocks.

blocks.alt: Packet Tracer topology with interface labels on every router and switch link.
blocks.caption: Interface labels from Packet Tracer: each router uses Gig0/0/0 for its LAN or switch, Gig0/0/1 and Gig0/0/2 for the WAN links.

blocks.text: Devices: three Cisco ISR4331 routers, three 2960-24TT switches, six PC-PT hosts (three per city), and two Server-PT DHCP servers. Router-to-router links are dashed in the diagram (RN1, RN2, RN3).

blocks.alt: Diagram showing each branch router with its ip helper-address pointing at the matching DHCP server behind Router-DC.
blocks.caption: Each branch router relays to its own server: Miami to 192.168.50.10 and New York to 192.168.50.20.

items: Discover: the client broadcasts (UDP 68 to UDP 67) because it has no address yet.
Relay: the city router receives it, writes its own LAN interface address into the giaddr field, and forwards the request as a unicast to the helper address.
Offer: the server compares giaddr to its scopes, picks the one that matches that subnet, and replies to the relay, which delivers it to the client.
Request and Acknowledge: the exchange finishes through the same relay and the client keeps the lease.

blocks.text: The relay only works if routing works in both directions. The Discover can reach the server and the Offer still gets lost without a return route.
New York DHCP server (192.168.50.20, gateway 192.168.50.1):

Scope math: the New York usable range is .65 to .126 (62 addresses). The first five (.65 to .69) are held back for the gateway and infrastructure, so the pool starts at .70 and serves 57 hosts. The server uses the gateway field for the client's default gateway, so it points at the branch router, not the DC router. The Miami server (192.168.50.10) follows the same pattern with gateway 192.168.0.1.

Commands in the order I used them. Each router starts at user mode; enable moves to privileged mode and configure terminal enters global configuration. Router prompts show the mode: > is user, # is privileged, (config)# is global configuration, and (config-if)# is interface configuration.
Router-DC (data center gateway for the servers):

enable
configure terminal
hostname Router-DC
no ip domain-lookup
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description Connected to SW-DC
 ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description Connected to Router-MIA
 ip address 10.0.2.2 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/2
 description Connected to Router-NY
 ip address 10.0.3.2 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
 exit
ip route 192.168.0.0 255.255.255.192 10.0.2.1
ip route 192.168.0.64 255.255.255.192 10.0.3.1
end
write memory
Router-MIA (Miami gateway and DHCP relay):

enable
configure terminal
hostname Router-MIA
no ip domain-lookup
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description Connected to SW-MIA
 ip address 192.168.0.1 255.255.255.192
 ip helper-address 192.168.50.10
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description Connected to Router-NY
 ip address 10.0.1.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/2
 description Connected to Router-DC
 ip address 10.0.2.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
 exit
ip route 192.168.0.64 255.255.255.192 10.0.1.2
ip route 192.168.50.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.2.2
end
write memory
Router-NY (New York gateway and DHCP relay):

enable
configure terminal
hostname Router-NY
no ip domain-lookup
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description Connected to SW-NY
 ip address 192.168.0.65 255.255.255.192
 ip helper-address 192.168.50.20
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description Connected to Router-MIA
 ip address 10.0.1.2 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/2
 description Connected to Router-DC
 ip address 10.0.3.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
 exit
ip route 192.168.0.0 255.255.255.192 10.0.1.1
ip route 192.168.50.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.3.2
end
write memory
Fixing a bad static route (the exact commands I used for the 194.168 and 193.168 typos):

configure terminal
no ip route 194.168.50.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.2.2
ip route 192.168.50.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.2.2
end
write memory
Changing the relay target on an interface:

configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 no ip helper-address 192.168.50.20
 ip helper-address 192.168.50.10
 end
write memory
Verification and troubleshooting commands on the routers:

rows: Current config, including interface addresses, helper addresses, and static routes
Saved config, to confirm write memory worked
Every interface with its IP address and up/up status
Routing table: C and L for connected networks, S for static routes
IP-to-MAC mappings the router has learned, such as a leased PC address
ICMP echo test; add repeat 5 to send five packets
Aborts a ping or other command that is hanging

blocks.text: Commands on the PCs (Desktop > Command Prompt) and servers:

rows: Leased address, mask, gateway, DHCP server, and DNS server
Drops the lease and requests a new one through the relay
Sends four ICMP echoes (use Ctrl+C to stop a hung ping)
Hop-by-hop path, which shows each router crossed
The PC's ARP table, which proves Layer 2 reachability to the gateway

blocks.text: Server steps (Desktop > Config and Services > DHCP in Packet Tracer): set the static IP, mask, gateway, and DNS under FastEthernet0; turn the DHCP service on; fill in the pool name, default gateway, DNS, start address, mask, and maximum users; then click Save. The scope is not active until it is saved.

rows: show ip interface brief (MIA, NY, DC)
Connected 192.168.50.0/24 and both /30 links, plus static routes to both city LANs
Replies across the MIA–DC link (first packet may drop while ARP resolves)
Address from the NY pool, gateway .65, DHCP server .20, DNS .20
PC's MAC listed for its leased address

blocks.text: Still to verify in this part: a Miami PC lease from 192.168.50.10, plus cross-site pings and traceroutes between the city gateways.

blocks.alt: Packet Tracer topology with green link-state triangles on every link.
blocks.caption: Every link shows green: all router, switch, PC, and server connections are up.

rows: Miami could not reach the DHCP server's subnet
Static route typed as 194.168.50.0 instead of 192.168.50.0
Removed it and added ip route 192.168.50.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.2.2
New York had no route back to the Miami LAN
Pings on PCs and routers hung for 10+ seconds
arp -a and show arp showed Layer 2 working
Packet Tracer was in Simulation mode, which animates every packet
Switched to Realtime mode; pings returned instantly
Re-read the command and the reply source
I had typed 192.168.0.6 instead of 192.168.0.65; the gateway answered, proving Layer 3 worked

blocks.text: Method: identify the problem, form a theory, test it, fix it, verify, and document. Reading the ARP tables on both ends ruled out Layer 2 before I went looking for the real cause.

items: DHCP and DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge), scopes, leases, and the gateway and DNS options a server hands out.
DHCP relay and giaddr, and why a router is the boundary of a broadcast domain.
UDP port 67 (server) and 68 (client). A client that cannot reach a server falls back to an APIPA address in 169.254.0.0/16.
Subnetting: /26 for LANs and /30 for point-to-point links, with usable ranges and broadcast addresses.
Static routing, and how one wrong octet breaks reachability.
ARP (IP to MAC), ICMP echo and destination unreachable, TTL (IOS routers reply with TTL 255), and traceroute.
The troubleshooting methodology, plus interface descriptions and saved configs as documentation habits.
A relay needs routes in both directions, not just toward the server.
The server picks a scope from the relay's interface subnet, so every scope must match a real LAN.
Save the pool on the server after editing it; an unsaved scope looks right on screen but serves nothing.
Check the tool before the network: Simulation mode looked like an outage.
Read unreachable replies carefully. The source address shows which device gave up.

blocks.text: Part 2 replaces the static routes with dynamic routing and repeats the same verification. This was built as part of my Enterprise Cloud Computing coursework; the troubleshooting and verification are my own work. Lab passwords, where used, are for lab use only, never production.

title: Lab 03 — Troubleshooting Speed Run: “I Can’t Reach the Website”
subtitle: Junior network engineer portfolio · Cisco Packet Tracer
status: Speed run · about 10 minutes · download and go
summary: A user cannot open a website, but a coworker can. Download the Packet Tracer file, skip the setup, and work the fault from the bottom up: link, IP config, gateway, routed path, name resolution. Each step shows the command, why it is run, what healthy looks like, and what a different result means.
imageAlt: Packet Tracer topology with a router, two switches, a server, and two PCs. Every link is green and each link shows its interface labels.
imageCaption: The lab network: R1 joins the user LAN (SW1) and the server LAN (SW2). SRV1 provides DNS and HTTP.

blocks.text: “I can’t get to Instagram from my computer. My coworker can.” You are the helpdesk. The network is already built. Find the fault, fix it, and prove it using the same layered method you would use on a real network.

items: Goal: restore access to http://instagram.com from PC1.
Time: about 10 minutes.
Rule: change nothing until you can state the cause in one sentence.

blocks.text: This is a speed run. Download the file and skip the setup. If you would rather build the network yourself, the steps are at the bottom of the page.

items: 1. Download the Packet Tracer file with the button at the top of the page and open it in Cisco Packet Tracer.
2. Switch to Realtime mode (bottom right) so pings return without the animation delay.
3. The network is already built and addressed. PC1 is the user with the ticket and PC2 is the coworker.
4. If PC1 can already open the site, reset the drill: open PC1, go to the Config tab, set the DNS server to 192.168.20.100, and close the window.
5. Open PC1 > Desktop > Command Prompt and start at Step 1 below.

blocks.alt: Packet Tracer topology with all links green and interface labels on every link.
blocks.caption: The lab network. The labels show the interface on each end of every link.

sections.title: The method: bottom up, stop at the first failure

blocks.text: Work the layers in order: link, IP configuration, gateway, routed path, name resolution. Run one test per layer. The first test that fails tells you which layer to fix. Change one thing at a time, then re-run the same test to prove it.
The six steps below are the whole lab. Everything else on the page supports them.

items: Run: Ask who else is affected, or test from a second PC.
Why: One affected user points to that computer’s settings. Everyone affected points to a shared part: the router, the switch, or the server.
Healthy: PC2 reaches the site and PC1 does not, so the fault is local to PC1.
If different: If PC2 fails too, look at the shared parts first: R1, SW1, and SRV1.
Run: Check the link light on PC1’s switch port, then run ipconfig /all in PC1’s Command Prompt.
Why: This confirms layer 1 and that PC1 has a valid address, mask, and gateway before you test anything else.
Healthy: A green link, IPv4 address 192.168.10.20, mask 255.255.255.0, and default gateway 192.168.10.1.

If different: An amber or red link means a cable or port problem. An address starting 169.254 means no address was assigned. A wrong mask or gateway breaks traffic to other subnets even when local pings work.

blocks.alt: Topology with every link showing a green triangle.
blocks.caption: Healthy links are green. Ports show amber for about 30 seconds while spanning tree settles, which is normal.

sections.title: Step 3 · Can PC1 reach its gateway?

items: Why: The gateway is the first hop. If PC1 cannot reach it, nothing beyond it can work.
Healthy: Four replies with TTL 255, which is the router answering.
If different: Timeouts mean the fault is on the user LAN or R1’s interface. Stop and fix layers 1 to 3 before you look at DNS.

blocks.alt: PC1 command prompt showing four replies from 192.168.10.1 with TTL 255.
blocks.caption: Healthy gateway ping: 4 of 4 replies, TTL 255.

sections.title: Step 4 · Can PC1 reach the server across the router?

items: Why: This proves the routed path and the server in one step, so you can rule routing in or out.
Healthy: Replies with TTL 127 from the server, and a trace that shows two hops: 192.168.10.1, then 192.168.20.10.

If different: If the gateway ping passed but this one fails, look at R1’s server-side interface, the route, SW2, or SRV1. A trace that stops at hop 1 points at R1. A trace that stops after hop 1 points at the server side.

blocks.text: The first ping can drop a packet while ARP resolves. Run it twice before you decide it failed.
On Windows the command is tracert. Typing traceroute returns “Invalid Command.”

blocks.alt: PC1 command prompt showing ipconfig output, an Invalid Command for traceroute, and a completed tracert with two hops.
blocks.caption: With the fault in place the trace still completes in two hops, so routing and the server are fine. The earlier traceroute attempt returned “Invalid Command” because Windows uses tracert.

sections.title: Step 5 · Can PC1 resolve the name?

items: Run: ping instagram.com, then check the DNS server in ipconfig /all or on PC1’s Config tab.
Why: If Step 4 passed, the network path is good. A failure by name points to name resolution.
Healthy: The ping reads “Pinging 192.168.20.10” and replies. The name was translated to the server’s address, and the DNS server setting is 192.168.20.10.
If different: If Packet Tracer reports it could not find the host while Step 4 passed, the problem is DNS. Here PC1’s DNS server is 192.168.20.100, an address nothing answers on.

blocks.alt: PC1 command prompt: ping 192.168.20.10 and ping instagram.com both get four replies from 192.168.20.10.
blocks.caption: Healthy: the name resolves to 192.168.20.10 and replies come back. The partial run at the top is the first ping, which dropped one packet while ARP resolved.

blocks.alt: PC1 Config tab showing default gateway 192.168.10.1 and DNS server 192.168.20.10.
blocks.caption: Healthy: PC1 asks the DNS server at 192.168.20.10.

blocks.alt: PC1 Config tab showing default gateway 192.168.10.1 and DNS server 192.168.20.100.
blocks.caption: The fault: PC1 asks 192.168.20.100, which does not exist, so no name resolves.

blocks.text: Key phrase: “Pings by IP work, pings by name fail, so DNS.”

sections.title: Step 6 · Fix it and prove it

items: Run: Set PC1’s DNS server to 192.168.20.10 on the Config tab, then run ping instagram.com and open http://instagram.com in the Web Browser.
Why: Re-run the exact test that failed. Never close the ticket on a guess.
Healthy: Replies from 192.168.20.10 and the page loads.
If different: If the name resolves but the page will not load, DNS is fixed and the next place to look is the HTTP service on SRV1 (Services > HTTP).

blocks.alt: Packet Tracer web browser showing the Cisco Packet Tracer test page at http://instagram.com.
blocks.caption: Success: the test page loads at http://instagram.com.

sections.title: What you see and what it means

rows: SW1 port, R1 Gi0/0, PC1 gateway and mask
Gateway ping works, server ping times out
PC1’s DNS server setting, then the DNS service on SRV1
Name resolves, page will not load

sections.title: Say it out loud: the 30-second version

blocks.text: “I’d start by confirming scope. Is it one user or the whole site? One user points to a local setting, not an outage. Next I’d check the link and the IP config. Then I’d test in layers: can it reach its gateway, and can it reach the server by IP across the router? If the IP path works and the name doesn’t resolve, that’s DNS, not routing. Then I’d fix the setting, verify with the same test that failed, and document what I found.”

rows: PC1 cannot open instagram.com. A coworker can.
Scope, link and IP config, gateway ping, server ping and tracert, name ping, DNS setting.
PC1’s DNS server was 192.168.20.100, which does not exist on the server subnet.
Re-ran ping instagram.com and loaded http://instagram.com.
What I would check first next time
The DNS server setting on the PC, right after confirming the IP path works.

sections.title: Design notes: why the server is on its own switch and subnet

blocks.text: Real networks keep servers apart from user desks. A server on its own switch means a user-side problem does not take the server down. A server on its own subnet means traffic to it crosses the router, so the DNS check in this lab also tests routing.

In an enterprise environment, DNS and web hosting would run on separate servers, so a DNS outage and a web outage can be told apart by which one fails. This lab combines them on SRV1 to keep the topology small.

items: DNS: name-to-address resolution, and why a PC with a bad DNS server can reach an IP but not a name.
Layered troubleshooting: link, IP config, gateway, routed path, name resolution, in that order.
TTL: 255 from the router and 127 from the server, a quick way to tell which device answered.
ICMP and tracert: echo replies, timeouts, and hop-by-hop path testing.
Verification: repeating the exact test that failed.

blocks.text: Skip this if you downloaded the file. Building the network takes about 10 minutes.

items: SW1 and SW2 are Cisco 2960-24TT switches. SW1 is the user switch and SW2 is the server switch.
All cables are copper straight-through.
PC1 Fa0 to SW1 Fa0/1, and PC2 Fa0 to SW1 Fa0/2.
R1 Gi0/1 to SW2 Gi0/1 (server LAN, 192.168.20.0/24).
SRV1 Fa0 to SW2 Fa0/1.

blocks.alt: Packet Tracer topology before configuration: the router links are red and the switch links are green.
blocks.caption: The topology before any configuration. The router ports are still shut down, so those links are red.

blocks.text: Configure R1 from its CLI tab. If Packet Tracer offers the initial configuration dialog, answer no.

enable
configure terminal
hostname R1
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description User LAN - to SW1 Gi0/1
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description Server LAN - to SW2 Gi0/1
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
end
show ip interface brief
Router ports are administratively down by default, so no shutdown is required. Both ports should read up and up.

items: SRV1: set the static address from the table. In Services, turn DNS on and add an A record for instagram.com pointing to 192.168.20.10. Keep HTTP on with index.html present.
PC1 and PC2: set static addresses from the table, with DNS 192.168.20.10.
Baseline check from PC1: ping 192.168.10.1, ping 192.168.20.10, ping instagram.com, then open http://instagram.com. All four should work before you break anything.
To start the drill, set PC1’s DNS server to 192.168.20.100.

title: Lab 04 — Inter-VLAN Routing on a Layer 3 Switch
subtitle: Junior network engineer portfolio · Cisco Packet Tracer
status: Build lab · about 30 minutes · no download yet
summary: Two departments share one building but sit in different VLANs and cannot reach each other. Turn a Layer 3 switch into their gateway: create VLANs, add an SVI per VLAN, enable ip routing, trunk to an access switch, and add a routed uplink to the edge router. Then break it three ways and fix it.
imageAlt: Topology: edge router R1 on top, Layer 3 switch MLS1 in the middle with SVIs for VLAN 10 and 20, access switch SW2 with PC1 and PC2 in VLAN 10 on a trunk, and PC3 and SRV1 in VLAN 20 on MLS1 access ports.
imageCaption: MLS1 (a Catalyst 3650 in Packet Tracer) routes between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 with SVIs and uplinks to R1 on a routed port.

blocks.text: “Sales (VLAN 10) can’t open the file server in Engineering (VLAN 20). They’re plugged into the same switch closet.” Same building, same switches, different VLANs: this is a routing problem, not a cabling one.

items: Goal: PC1 in VLAN 10 can ping SRV1 in VLAN 20, and both VLANs can reach R1.
Rule: routing happens on MLS1 (the Layer 3 switch), not by adding a router-on-a-stick.

blocks.text: Before you start, predict: when PC1 pings SRV1, which device rewrites the MAC addresses and lowers the TTL? (Answer at the end.)

sections.title: Step 1: Build VLANs and SVIs on MLS1

blocks.text:
enable
configure terminal
hostname MLS1
vlan 10
 name SALES
vlan 20
 name ENGINEERING
exit
!
interface range gigabitEthernet1/0/2 - 3
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
!
interface vlan 10
 ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
interface vlan 20
 ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
!
ip routing

items: vlan 10 / vlan 20 create the VLANs in the VLAN database.
interface vlan 10 creates the SVI: the Layer 3 gateway for VLAN 10.
ip routing turns the switch's routing engine on. Leave it out on purpose later in the break/fix.

sections.title: Step 2: Trunk to the access switch

blocks.text:
! MLS1
interface gigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
 switchport mode trunk
!
! SW2
enable
configure terminal
hostname SW2
vlan 10
 name SALES
interface gigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
interface range fastEthernet0/1 - 2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10

On many Layer 3 switches (including the 3560 in Packet Tracer) the trunk will not form until you set switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q. Newer models support only 802.1Q and do not need the command.

! MLS1
interface gigabitEthernet1/0/24
 no switchport
 ip address 10.1.99.2 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.1.99.1
!
! R1
interface gigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.99.1 255.255.255.252
 no shutdown
ip route 10.1.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.1.99.2
ip route 10.1.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.1.99.2
no switchport turns the port into a routed port, so it behaves like a router interface. R1 needs static routes back to both VLAN subnets, or replies from R1 would have nowhere to go.

rows: VLAN 10 and 20 exist; access ports listed in the right VLAN
Gi1/0/1 trunking, encapsulation 802.1q, VLAN 10 allowed and active
Vlan10, Vlan20, and Gi1/0/24 are up/up with the right IPs
Replies. The first may time out while ARP resolves.
First hop 10.1.10.1 (the SVI), then the server: one routed hop

sections.title: Step 5: Break it, then fix it

rows: PC1 can ping 10.1.10.1 but not SRV1
SVIs answer locally, but the switch no longer routes between them
PC1 can reach PC2 but nothing off its subnet
The gateway must be in the host's own subnet: the VLAN 10 SVI
Vlan10 SVI goes down/down on MLS1; VLAN 10 is isolated
An SVI needs at least one active port or trunk in its VLAN
VLAN 20 cannot ping R1; VLAN 10 still can
Pings reach R1, but R1 has no return path

blocks.text: Work each break bottom up: is the link up (show interfaces trunk), is the SVI up (show ip interface brief), is routing on (show ip route), is the host's gateway right (ipconfig)?

items: Answer to the warm-up: MLS1 rewrites the MAC addresses and decrements the TTL. The IP addresses of PC1 and SRV1 never change.
Compare with router-on-a-stick: the same result, but every inter-VLAN packet would cross one router link twice.
Interview line: “I configured inter-VLAN routing on a Layer 3 switch with SVIs and a routed uplink, then troubleshot SVI, trunk, gateway, and return-route failures.”

blocks.text: Study notes: Layer 2 Switches, Layer 3 Switches, and Routers (Network+), and Chapter 11 for VLANs and trunks.

title: Display-path isolation
subtitle: A+ Core 1 · 220-1201 objective 5.3
summary: Choose and interpret one display test at a time, restore the setup, then solve a different audio fault. Use equipment or the complete paper alternative.

sections.title: Prepare and record your first reasoning

blocks.text: Goal: isolate an input/cable fault, verify the fix, and transfer the reasoning to an audio fault. Read the display-troubleshooting notes first, especially Input, cables, and adapter direction. Use an authorized computer and external display with known-good connections, or use the paper alternative below.

items: Equipment route: save work and record original input, display mode, audio output, and cable connections. Use only accessible external controls and compatible ports/cables. Do not change drivers, damage cables, block vents, open a lamp, or simulate overheating.
Paper route: no equipment is required. Write your chosen test and predicted result before reading each result section. Cover later sections with paper or scroll one section at a time.
Record first answer, hint use, retries, observed result, and final explanation separately. This written exercise awards no points and stores no progress; use your own worksheet.

blocks.text: Authored setup: the display is powered, its own menu is readable, the computer is sending a Duplicate image, and the cable enters HDMI 1. The display is set to HDMI 2 and says “no signal.” Choose between selecting HDMI 1, replacing the display, or reinstalling Windows. Write why your test is the best first step.

Equipment route: if your display has an unused selectable input, temporarily select it to reproduce the mismatch, then choose the input actually connected. If it does not support this, use the paper result. Do not disconnect your only usable screen.

Hint 1: compare a setting you can observe directly with the physical connection. Hint 2: the listening input and connected socket have different numbers. Hints have no score cost; record whether you used them.

Paper result: selecting HDMI 1 restores the image without changing the cable or computer. Evidence → input mismatch; decision → select the connected input; consequence → picture restored. This supports an input-selection explanation; it does not prove all hardware can never fail.

If you chose replacement or OS reinstall, explain why neither was required by this evidence. Return to Case 1, choose the input test, and record a retry rather than erasing the first answer. Equipment route: record what actually happened, even if it differs; do not invent a successful result.

Authored paper evidence: the correct input and supported mode are selected, but the image flashes with cable A. With the source, ports, display, and mode unchanged, a known-good compatible cable B produces a stable image. What does this implicate, and what remains unproven?

Equipment route: with permission, compare two known-compatible cables under the same conditions. Do not create a damaged cable or expect healthy equipment to flash. If both work, record “fault not reproduced” and reason from the paper evidence separately.

Hint 1: list the variables held constant. Hint 2: only the cable changed in the paper case. Feedback: the evidence implicates cable A’s path; it does not justify replacing the panel or claiming every driver is healthy. If you overclaimed, revise your conclusion and record a retry.

Before reading the next section, answer without hints: another projector has working built-in speakers and a clear HDMI picture. A known audio sample plays through the laptop speakers because those are the selected output. The projector is unmuted. Choose your next test, predict the result, and say why replacing the video cable is weaker.

Equipment route: only if your external display has speakers, play a quiet sample and compare the intended output with laptop speakers using the OS audio selector. Restore the original audio output afterward. Otherwise use the paper case.

Paper result: selecting the projector’s audio output makes the sample audible from its speakers. The changed fault is audio routing, not input selection. Video and audio need separate verification. Review the notes section “Video works, but audio does not” and flashcard fc-core1-display-08 if you missed this.

If you needed feedback before giving your answer, mark the attempt assisted. For another unaided check, explain what changes when the display has no speakers and the video path is VGA. Expected reasoning: VGA carries no audio; choose an appropriate separate speaker connection and verify it, rather than expecting the video cable to provide sound.

items: Restore original input, display mode, audio output, and connections. Confirm the normal image and intended sound work. Do not report a paper result as an observation of physical equipment.

Complete your record: evidence → chosen test → actual or supplied result → decision → consequence → what remains uncertain. For intermittent symptoms, describe how long you observed rather than claiming permanent repair.

Review input/cable mistakes in notes sections Input, cables, and adapter direction and Flashing screens and incorrect colors; review audio mistakes in Video works, but audio does not. Record completion separately from unaided transfer success.

Acceptance: justify the input test, hold conditions constant during cable substitution, avoid unsupported panel/driver conclusions, select and verify an audio output, and restore settings. Successful completion is practice evidence, not an exam-readiness score.

title: Defensive evidence triage
subtitle: Network+ · Chapter 21 · Written exercise
summary: Use fictional lease, ARP, and resolver evidence to choose a bounded response. No attack tools, live traffic, or production changes are required.

blocks.text: Paper alternative: copy the evidence and response columns onto paper. A text editor works too. Allow 20–30 minutes; no software installation, packet injection, passwords, or access to a real network is needed. Prerequisites: DHCP options, local ARP, DNS, and VLAN boundaries.

For each phase, write observation → theory → next discriminating check → least disruptive authorized action → validation. Record your first answer before opening the hints or reading the debrief below. This is self-checked written practice; the site does not score or save it.

rows: A lease from 10.21.10.77 supplies gateway 10.21.10.77 and resolver 10.21.10.77.
An older valid lease still uses the approved options.
10.21.10.77 is traced to an unapproved desktop service on an access port.

blocks.text: Write your leading mechanism and the two strongest supporting observations. Choose one next check and an authorized containment action. Explain why this does not yet demonstrate ARP poisoning. Do not assume every record is malicious just because it differs from a baseline.

sections.title: 3. New evidence: test a second theory

blocks.text: Reveal after your first decision: the approved gateway’s ARP binding remains unchanged on both clients. A resolver log on the unauthorized service records a substituted payroll answer; there is no evidence that the approved resolver’s cache changed. The response lead authorizes isolating the unapproved service while retaining evidence.

Revise your theory. Is DNS response spoofing supported? Is poisoning of the approved resolver established? Describe how to restore approved client settings and verify an allowed service after containment. Name one thing still unknown; do not conclude an on-path relay occurred without evidence that traffic was forwarded.

sections.title: 4. Progressive hints and a recoverable retry

items: Hint 1: Compare the lease source and options before inspecting application symptoms. Which source supplied the route and resolver?
Hint 2: ARP poisoning needs a false IP-to-MAC binding; a changed DHCP router option is a different observation.
Hint 3: A false answer from an unauthorized resolver is not evidence that the approved resolver cached it. Choose controls for the demonstrated mechanism.

blocks.text: If stuck, retain your first response, note the hint number, and retry with a different evidence-based explanation. Reading a debrief is assisted completion; do not overwrite your first attempt or call it mastery.

rows: Unauthorized leases change router and DNS options.
Treat rogue DHCP as the leading supported mechanism; preserve lease and source-port records, then isolate as authorized.
Prevent further offers while retaining evidence. Review DHCP snooping against approved server/relay paths before applying it.
Do not label this record ARP poisoning.
Use additional captures or change records if a competing theory remains.
DNS spoofing is supported; poisoning of the approved cache is unproven.
Restore approved settings through the response process, renew affected leases, and verify resolver, route, and legitimate application identity.
Verify approved clients still receive valid leases and can reach required services.
Check both a permitted service and a prohibited path. Investigate any remaining symptoms separately.

blocks.text: A strong response names the evidence, preserves it, constrains the action to authorization, and checks recovery. Clearing every cache or resetting every switch first destroys context and can introduce outages. Review the related DHCP, switch, security, and Chapter 21 notes below before retrying.

A different client has an approved lease and uses the approved resolver. Captures now show forged ARP replies associating the real gateway IP with an unauthorized MAC. Write a fresh theory, the distinguishing evidence, a suitable control to evaluate, and one benign possibility you would rule out. Complete this without the earlier hints.

Self-check after answering: false ARP messages and a changed cache support ARP poisoning. Validate against gateway redundancy and authorized changes, locate the source, and evaluate dynamic ARP inspection with correct trusted bindings and static-host handling. DHCP snooping alone is not a promise that every ARP message is validated.

items: Explain why changed lease options, false ARP bindings, and poisoned DNS cache entries are different evidence.
Choose a mechanism-specific control and state at least one limitation or deployment assumption.
Record first attempt, hint use, revision, and unaided transfer separately.
Verify recovery and boundary policy with allowed and denied cases; identify what the evidence still cannot establish.

blocks.text: All addresses, logs, sequence, authorizations, and results in this exercise are authored assumptions. There is no real incident, attack execution, automated grading, or demonstrated learner-outcome measurement.

title: Model-specific laptop inspection and service plan
subtitle: A+ Core 1 · Chapter 4 · Paper-first service planning
summary: Use an official Surface Laptop 7th Edition service guide to plan safe inspections and distinguish evidence from a replacement decision. No device is opened or battery handled.

blocks.text: Paper alternative: print this page or record your answers on paper after consulting the named official Microsoft service guide. Allow about 20 minutes. Allow about 20 minutes. This is a planning exercise only: do not open a real laptop, touch a damaged battery, order a part, or perform a calibration cycle.

Scenario: a help-desk ticket says “laptop shuts down early; battery indicator says 40%; one key sometimes repeats.” The device is identified as a Microsoft Surface Laptop 7th Edition. Preserve the user’s work and record the exact report before deciding which component, if any, needs service.

Primary guide: Microsoft, Surface Laptop 7th Edition Component Disassembly and Reassembly. The repair portal says to read the safety instructions and the model guide before service. Procedures and part lists apply to this model only; they are not generic directions for other laptops.

rows: Ticket: early shutdown, displayed 40%, repeating key
Two symptoms are reported; neither alone identifies a failed battery or keyboard.
A model/OS health indicator warrants the documented diagnostic/service path; it is not a universal capacity percentage rule.
This model’s diagnostic supports service follow-up. Do not substitute a generic full-discharge routine.
External keyboard types normally; one built-in key repeats
The symptom is localized to built-in input but does not yet distinguish key mechanism, debris, connector, or keyboard assembly.
No heat, odor, swelling, leakage, or case deformation is reported
No battery damage sign is stipulated. Do not infer that every battery is safe from absence in a ticket; actual inspection belongs to trained authorized service under the vendor guide.

blocks.text: Write: observation → plausible theory → next discriminating check → what evidence would justify a part replacement → post-service verification. Name at least one fact you still do not know.

items: Open the official Microsoft Surface Service Guide Center and the Surface Laptop 7th Edition component guide. Locate the warning that the guide, compatible parts and specified tools are required.
In the battery inspection section, identify examples of damage signs (for example expansion, leaking, discoloration, odor, dents, or damaged wires). What is the stop condition if any appears?
Find the guide’s device-specific battery setup/repair validation references. Explain why that does not authorize a generic “drain to zero to calibrate” procedure on an unrelated laptop.
For the repeating key, use the exact model part list to determine whether a key, keyboard, top case, or full assembly is supported; do not assume an individual key is orderable.

blocks.text: Write the source section or page title next to each finding. If the site changes or the guide is unavailable, record the source as unverified and stop short of a procedure claim.
First attempt: choose one next step for the battery symptom and one for the key symptom. Do not combine symptoms into a single guessed part. Record your answer before opening the hint.

items: Hint 1: compare the exact model’s built-in battery result with the manufacturer’s service path. A charge percentage is not a chemical-capacity repair.
Hint 2: test the input with a reversible external keyboard and check the model’s diagnostics/parts list before opening the device.
Hint 3: a damage sign changes the plan from normal inspection to the vendor’s battery-safety stop/escalation. Never manipulate a swollen cell.

blocks.text: Retry: keep your first answer, state which hint changed your reasoning, and write a narrower decision. A hint-assisted answer is practice evidence, not proof of mastery.

rows: Battery status + model diagnostic recommends action
Battery service is supported for this model by the diagnostic; the exercise does not promise repair outcome.
Follow the exact guide, compatible parts, safety checklist and required battery validation or send for qualified service.
Built-in key repeats; external keyboard works
Input fault is more localized, but exact failed part remains undetermined.
Use model diagnostics/parts list, inspect only if authorized and safe, then test all keys and user workflow after service.
Do not charge, press, bend or puncture. Follow manufacturer and local battery-safety handling/disposal directions.
A part installation alone does not prove success.
Run vendor diagnostics and required model-specific calibration/validation; confirm battery reporting, charging, keyboard behavior and data/user workflow.

blocks.text: There is no physical-device action, scored result, automatic learner tracking, or observed repair outcome in this exercise. All ticket observations are authored assumptions; the cited vendor guide supplies only the model-specific procedure boundary.

A different manufacturer’s laptop has a dim display. The attachment’s old answer key says “replace the inverter.” Without opening the device, list the exact model/specification evidence you would seek to determine whether it has a CCFL inverter, an LED driver, or an OLED panel. Then give one reversible check and one reason not to promise that a display assembly replacement will solve it.

items: Use a model-specific manufacturer guide rather than a generic teardown.
Separate symptom, test evidence, theory, part compatibility and replacement threshold.
Identify when battery damage requires stopping and escalating.
Explain why battery gauge calibration is vendor/model-specific and cannot restore worn capacity.
Name post-service checks for both the battery and keyboard.

title: Plan and troubleshoot a small SOHO network
subtitle: A+ Core 1 · Chapter 9 · Paper-first network lab
summary: Choose safe wireless settings, assign fictional IPv4 details, and isolate DHCP, gateway, DNS and weak-signal symptoms without changing a live router.

blocks.text: Paper alternative: copy each table and fill the blank decision column in a notebook. No router login, radio scan, account, external network or software installation is required. All addresses, service options, observed settings and user needs below are fictional.

A four-person design office is moving into a small suite. The provider has installed an ONT. The office has a router/firewall with an integrated switch and access point, one wired printer, two wired workstations and two wireless laptops. Your job is to plan a reversible setup in a worksheet and diagnose three staged client reports.

Approved plan facts: LAN IPv4 network 192.168.40.0/24; router LAN gateway 192.168.40.1; internal DNS resolver 192.168.40.53; DHCP pool 192.168.40.100–192.168.40.149; printer reserved at 192.168.40.20. A helper may use 192.168.40.10 for a temporary static test only after confirming no conflict. The ISP offers fiber 300/300 Mbps or cable 1000/35 Mbps; this office frequently uploads large design files.

rows: Internet handoff from ONT to router WAN
Use the WAN/internet interface named in the router and ISP guides.
Use a non-identifying SSID and an approved security mode/client-compatible passphrase.
Check client bands, country/regulatory setting, AP support and local channel scan.
Change default admin credentials; use supported firmware and a documented recovery method.
Keep router/gateway, DNS and reserved printer outside dynamic pool as specified.
Use DHCP for ordinary clients; only enter a static address for the authorized diagnostic case.
If needed, use a separate guest option and test that it cannot reach office devices.

blocks.text: Select fiber for the stated upload-heavy workflow from these two fictional offers, but explain why that choice does not establish that fiber is always faster than cable in every market. A correctly secured setup should not depend on changing the SSID name for encryption.

sections.title: 3. Stage one: no usable DHCP lease

rows: Connected to the approved SSID; signal is strong.
Service enabled; scope shows 38 leases remaining; no offer is recorded for Laptop A.

blocks.text: Write the most supported layer to investigate, one next check and one validation. Do not call this a DNS fault when no resolver was obtained. A 169.254/16 address signals an unusable automatic IPv4 lease but does not prove the DHCP server itself is broken.

sections.title: 4. Stage two: local and off-subnet reachability

rows: 192.168.40.20; responds to a same-LAN test from another workstation
Laptop B cannot reach 192.168.40.1 or the internet.

blocks.text: Identify the conflicting value and explain why a same-LAN printer test can still work when the default gateway is wrong. State how to restore the approved DHCP configuration and verify the router path. Do not change the router or printer addresses.

sections.title: 5. Stage three: IP works, names do not

rows: An approved numeric-address test to a known service succeeds; a name lookup for that service times out.
The resolver administrator reports a maintenance outage; no alternate resolver is approved in this scenario.

blocks.text: Name the failed layer and the authorized next action. Do not set a public DNS server or bypass the approved resolver without permission. State what should be tested after the resolver is restored.

sections.title: 6. Stage four: weak service in the conference room

blocks.text: A laptop in the conference room has a supported 2.4/5 GHz radio. The AP’s 5 GHz signal is weak through two walls; the 2.4 GHz signal is stronger. A scan shows a permitted 20 MHz channel with less local contention on 2.4 GHz than the currently crowded 5 GHz channel.

Choose a first test from the supplied evidence and state what you would measure. Consider band, channel, width, AP placement and client support. Do not claim that 2.4 GHz is always faster, or assign channels outside the router’s country setting. A client/AP change is only a plan; the exercise applies no live setting.

items: Hint 1: no lease means address configuration is the first layer; a wrong gateway is different from a wrong DNS resolver.
Hint 2: traffic to a same-subnet printer may not need the default gateway; off-subnet traffic does.
Hint 3: when the numeric-address test works but the approved name lookup fails, follow the DNS evidence and authorization boundary.
Hint 4: choose a band/channel from the client capability, measured RF conditions and local regulatory settings; a memorized 1/6/11 answer is not globally valid.

blocks.text: Retry each stage after writing the first answer. Keep the original, record which hint was used, and explain what evidence changed your decision.

rows: 169.254/16 and no gateway or DNS; no DHCP offer recorded
Investigate client association and DHCP service/scope/path before assigning cause.
Obtain an approved lease in the expected range with correct mask, gateway and resolver; then test gateway and name resolution.
Restore the approved .1 gateway through DHCP; a same-subnet printer can still be reachable.
Check local printer, gateway, off-subnet path and approved DNS separately.
Gateway and numeric destination work; name lookup fails during resolver outage
Follow resolver incident process; do not add an unapproved external resolver.
Repeat approved DNS lookup and named application test after service restoration.
Weak 5 GHz across walls; stronger, less-contended 2.4 GHz offered
Test the supported 2.4 GHz plan; compare signal and actual application throughput.
Check local regulatory limits, channel scan, width, AP/client support and user workload.

blocks.text: A successful path is not verified by a single ping. Record permitted and intended application checks, and confirm the guest boundary if configured. All output is simulated; no real router, account or network was changed.

A guest phone has a valid address, gateway and resolver and can browse the internet, but it can also reach a file share on the staff LAN. Write the evidence that distinguishes an addressing problem from a missing guest boundary, the least disruptive configuration review, and the allowed/denied tests that would verify the policy.

items: Fill in the addressing roles for IP/mask, gateway, DNS, DHCP, reservation and APIPA.
Distinguish a missing DHCP lease, wrong gateway and failed DNS resolution using the supplied observations.
Select a WLAN band/channel plan with explicit client and regional constraints.
Explain why an SSID change, MAC filter, or NAT alone does not replace secure WLAN authentication and firewall policy.
Complete the changed guest-boundary transfer case and record what the evidence does not establish.
